en: Mayon Volcano has a perfect cone shape because its highly viscous lava cools quickly and piles up near the vent instead of flowing far.
Slightly acidic rainwater slowly dissolves the limestone bedrock of Palawan, carving out the massive caverns of the Puerto Princesa Subterranean River National Park.
The Zambales Mountains block the moisture-rich Habagat monsoon winds, forcing the air upward to cool and drop heavy rain on western Luzon.
Magma beneath Albay heats underground water into steam, which rises through wells to spin turbines and generate electricity at the Tiwi Geothermal Power Plant.
Cold nighttime air sinks into the valleys around Mount Pulag, trapping moisture below the peak to create a thick sea of clouds at sunrise.
Millions of tiny coral polyps in the Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park extract calcium from seawater to build hard limestone skeletons, forming massive reef structures.
During high tide, the elevated water level of Manila Bay pushes seawater backward into the Pasig River, temporarily reversing its natural eastward flow.
Heavy monsoon rains in the Caraballo Mountains cause the Cagayan River to overflow because the narrow northern coastal plains cannot quickly drain the excess water.
The ancient eruption of Taal Volcano collapsed its magma chamber, forming a large caldera that later filled with rainwater to create Lake Taal.
The narrow shape of the Verde Island Passage accelerates ocean currents, bringing abundant nutrients that support its status as the center of marine biodiversity.
Millions of years of wind and rain weathered the uplifted coral limestone of Bohol, leaving behind the distinct, symmetrical mounds of the Chocolate Hills.
Farmers carved terraced flat areas into the steep Ifugao mountains to slow down rainwater runoff, preventing soil erosion while irrigating their rice crops.
